newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Blair and Jiang pledge to build new relationship.
newsitem.headline: Blair and Jiang pledge to build new relationship.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair, given a rousing reception by the people of Hong Kong, said it was time for Britain and China to put past battles behind them and build a new relationship after the handover of Hong Kong.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin, who flew into Hong Kong on Monday for historic ceremonies to end 156 years of colonial rule, officially invited Blair to visit China and both leaders appeared eager to build closer ties.

"We want a relationship based on the 21st century, putting the battles and struggles of the past behind us," Blair told Jiang during a 45-minute meeting, shown live on television, held at a harbourfront hotel before they both attended formal handover ceremonies.
Blair, who flew into Hong Kong for a lightning 13-hour visit, told the Chinese leader: "Hong Kong can become a bridge rather than a barrier between Britain and China."
The two countries have locked horns in the build-up to the handover with China vilifying outgoing governor Chris Patten for bringing democratic reforms to Hong Kong.
Britain in turn said China was overreacting by planning to send 4,000 troops into Hong Kong just hours after the handover.
"This is an historic moment for China, Britain and Hong Kong and it can mark a new beginning in our relationship," Blair said in the meeting.
Officials were at pains to stress that the two leaders had a genuinely positive and friendly meeting with the 70-year-old Jiang even joking with Blair, 46, about his youth.
Jiang told the new prime minister: "If there is one thing I have to admire about you, it is that you're a young man. It is pointless to be jealous."
During their talks, the two leaders talked about the problems of jet lag and how humid it can get in Beijing, with Jiang saying to Blair: "It is my sincere hope you will come to China again."
The official Chinese news agency Xinhua said Blair "accepted the invitation with pleasure".
The Labour Party leader, who went to China while in opposition in 1988, in turn gave the Chinese leader an elegantly bound collection of the complete works of William Shakespeare.

The British prime minister, mobbed like a rock star by thousands of local Chinese as he went on a walkabout at a giant shopping mall, earlier held talks with Tung Chee-hwa, hand-picked by Beijing to be Hong Kong's future leader.
British officials said Blair stressed the need for free and fair elections for a new legislature and won reassurances from Tung that these would be held by next May at the latest.

A democratically elected legislative council, Britain's farewell gift to Hong Hong and target of Sino-British bickering, is being scrapped by China on the handover and replaced by a Beijing-anointed provisional chamber.
In talks with both Tung and Jiang, Blair said it was essential that China adhered to the 1984 Joint Declaration that guarantees the future prosperity and freedom of Hong Kong for the next 50 years.
Blair, underlying the historic nature of his visit, told reporters: "As we leave Hong Kong a chapter in our history is closing. But we must write a new chapter."
